stimulus.title: Proposal: A Neighbourhood Tool Library at Oakwood Hall
stimulus.body:
Dear Oakwood Community Committee,

I am writing to propose establishing a volunteer-run Neighbourhood Tool Library in the unused storeroom at the back of Oakwood Hall. Most households own a drill, a ladder, or hedge shears that sit idle in a shed for eleven months of the year. By pooling donated and grant-funded tools into a shared lending catalogue, residents could borrow what they need for a weekend project for a modest annual membership fee of twenty dollars.

Beyond saving families money and garage space, a tool library reduces unnecessary manufacturing and brings neighbours together. Saturday morning borrowing hours could also host short, free repair clinics where skilled retirees teach younger residents how to sharpen secateurs or mend a wobbly chair. To address safety and maintenance, every borrower would sign a simple care agreement, and power tools would be inspected and tagged quarterly by a qualified electrician. I would welcome the chance to present a detailed budget at next month's meeting.

Exam technique: verify 'In the unused storeroom at the back of Oakwood Hall' directly against the passage and rule out distractors that distort scope or tone.
reviewFocus: Verify passage evidence, Australian English, and absence of defensible distractor readings.

stimulus.title: Reading the Land: How Contour Lines Work
stimulus.body: A flat paper map faces an obvious puzzle: how can two dimensions show the rise and fall of hills, valleys and cliffs? Cartographers solve this using contour lines—imaginary lines drawn on a map that connect all points at the exact same height above sea level. The vertical height difference between one contour line and the next is called the contour interval, which on standard bushwalking maps is often ten metres. By studying how closely these lines are packed together, a hiker can read the steepness of the terrain at a glance. When contour lines are spaced far apart, the slope is gentle and easy to walk; when they crowd tightly together, the ground rises sharply into a steep ridge or cliff. Loops of concentric contour lines indicate a hilltop or peak, whereas V-shaped bends pointing uphill usually mark a gully or creek bed. Checking the contour pattern before setting off helps walkers estimate both physical effort and travel time—a five-kilometre track across flat contours takes far less time than five kilometres climbing fifty contour intervals.

The vertical height difference between one contour line and the next is called the contour interval, which on standard bushwalking maps is often ten metres. By studying how closely these lines are packed together, a hiker can read the steepness of the terrain at a glance. When contour lines are spaced far apart, the slope is gentle and easy to walk; when they crowd tightly together, the ground rises sharply into a steep ridge or cliff. Loops of concentric contour lines indicate a hilltop or peak, whereas V-shaped bends pointing uphill usually mark a gully or creek bed. Checking the contour pattern before setting off helps walkers estimate both physical effort and travel time—a five-kilometre track across flat contours takes far less time than five kilometres climbing fifty contour intervals.
